And it is not lawful for them that they should conceal that which Allah hath created in their wombs if they are believers in Allah and the Last Day. And their husbands would do better to take them back in that case if they desire a reconciliation. And they (women) have rights similar to those (of men) over them in kindness, and men are a degree above them. Allah is Mighty, Wise

105:3.en: And send against them swarms of flying creatures

haen68_BSoE.speaker: adnan
haen68_BSoE.speaker_note: his series voice; refers to earlier sessions of Facing Disbelief and his own past series
haen68_BSoE.title: Facing Disbelief 5: Scientific Mentions in the Quran, Prophetic Traditions, and the Problem of Evil
haen68_BSoE.one_line: How to handle scientific objections to the Quran and hadith, why 'scientific miracles' weaken faith, how to weigh ahad hadith, and why evil exists.
haen68_BSoE.summary: He takes on the scientific objections people raise against Islam. Many come from reading a verse the way the critic wants and then attacking that reading: the sun's course, the six days of creation, Nuh's flood, Hawa from the rib, the splitting of the moon, and supposed flaws in the human body. He argues that religion explains the why behind things rather than the how, that the Quran never says the flood covered the earth, that the rib and hastiness are metaphors, that the moon verse speaks of the approach of the Hour, and that the best stature in Surat al-Tin is about function and purpose, not physical perfection. He then warns against building faith on so-called scientific and numerical miracles, which collapse and push people out of the deen, and calls this a symptom of an ummah desperate for Western validation. Next he lays out classes of evidence: the Quran is mass-transmitted and fully authentic, while ahad hadith carry a human margin of error, so a hard narration can be left aside without being defended or rejected. Finally he treats the problem of evil: it rests on our own expectations of what God should do, Muslims never struggled with it as Christians did, good is only valued against its opposite, and Allah promised accountability in the Hereafter and charged us with lifting oppression. He asks people to see every event as a test.

outline.heading: Opening
The sun running to its resting place
outline.gist: Critics read the verse as the sun circling the earth; the sun does travel through space, and the verse also describes what a person observes.

outline.heading: The sun prostrating under the Throne: religion explains the why
outline.gist: The hadith can only be read metaphorically; religion speaks to meaning and purpose, not the mechanics science studies, and forcing one onto the other is our own error.

outline.heading: Six days of creation
outline.gist: The Arabic word for day means an undefined period; scholars knew these were not our days long before science, and six signals a long time.

outline.heading: The flood of Nuh was local
outline.gist: The Quran never says the flood covered the whole earth, only Nuh's people; the global flood comes from altered biblical texts, a lesson in how precise revelation is and how human tampering creates problems.

outline.heading: Hawa from the rib and man created of haste
outline.gist: Both are figures of speech: woman comes from the same substance as man and is close to his heart, and humans are by nature impatient.

outline.heading: The splitting of the moon: a sign of the Hour
outline.gist: Many scholars read the verse as an event before the Day of Judgment; the Quran often speaks of future events in the past tense.

outline.heading: The moon hadith narrated by one companion
outline.gist: A public miracle would have been seen and cited by many companions, unlike the twenty or more who narrated the multiplying of Jabir's food; he believes something happened but not as commonly imagined.

outline.heading: Supposed flaws in human design and the Nirvana fallacy
outline.gist: Calling the appendix or limited eyesight a mistake sets a made-up standard of perfection and projects it onto the Creator.

outline.heading: The best stature means fitness for purpose
outline.gist: Taqwim refers to function: humans have every faculty their task requires; vestigial remnants of a long creation do not deny Allah, and an unknown benefit is not an absent one.

outline.heading: Scientific miracles as a weak foundation for iman
outline.gist: Faith built on a claimed scientific miracle falls when the claim falls, a leading reason people leave the deen.

outline.heading: The ant and glass claim
outline.gist: A fabricated claim that the ant's word in Surat al-Naml pointed to glass-like bodies collapsed once checked.

outline.heading: No lie ever serves the truth
outline.gist: Well-meant fabrications, like forged hadith in the past, never help; only the narrow exceptions are allowed.

outline.heading: The mite on the mosquito's head
outline.gist: The verse means something smaller than a mosquito; the 'on top of its head' reading is linguistically impossible and accepted only out of thirst for proof.

outline.heading: The moon crater claim
outline.gist: The story that NASA found a split in the moon was invented; people who built faith on it fell hard.

outline.heading: The real sources of iman
outline.gist: Iman should rest on the universe, life, history and personal experience, which never change.

outline.heading: Numerical miracles and the Quran's real purpose
outline.gist: The Quran is a book of sociology, psychology and law, not biology or math; mining it for theories and numbers is a lack of adab with Allah.

outline.heading: An ummah desperate for validation
outline.gist: The hunt for miracles came from spiritual weakness and a wish to impress Western atheists, though Islam's description of God is the only one that holds up.

outline.heading: Predicting the future from verse numbers
outline.gist: Calculations that predict the fall of countries are disrespectful to the book.

outline.heading: You do not have to defend every hadith
outline.gist: The Quran is mass-transmitted and fully authentic; that is what must be defended.

outline.heading: Classes of evidence
outline.gist: Clear Quranic text, Quranic text open to more than one meaning, and ahad narrations where the chain rests on one person at some point.

outline.heading: Two extremes on hadith
outline.gist: Rejecting all hadith and treating all evidence as equal are both forms of legal suicide.

outline.heading: Checking chain and text, and suspending judgment
outline.gist: Scholars judged both the isnad and the matn; when a sound narration cannot be made sense of, you pause and leave it rather than reject it.

outline.heading: A human margin of error
outline.gist: Even a two percent error rate in Bukhari would be a handful of narrations; mistakes in hearing, seeing or wording are normal in human effort, so hard hadith are no argument against Islam.

outline.heading: Why the problem of evil grew
outline.gist: It is a leading reason people leave faith, especially in the Middle East after the Arab Spring and the cruelty of regimes.

outline.heading: Mackie's argument rests on our expectations
outline.gist: The logical problem of evil assumes we define what good is and what God must do, projecting our values onto Allah.

outline.heading: Watching suffering in real time
outline.gist: Live-streamed global suffering overwhelms people in a way local suffering never did.

outline.heading: The Christian God versus Allah's balanced description
outline.gist: The problem grew from a God described as all-loving to all; the Quran also speaks of punishment and those Allah does not love, so Muslims never struggled with it.

outline.heading: Asking why He did not create a world without evil
outline.gist: The question assumes we understand what creating a meaningful universe requires, which is arrogant.

outline.heading: Good is valued only against its opposite
outline.gist: Those born without a faculty do not miss it, as in Helen Keller's life; pain and evil let us value mercy, love and ease.

outline.heading: The child raised with a silver spoon
outline.gist: A child who never knew hardship cannot value what he has.

outline.heading: Nature is cruel, and Adam's lesson
outline.gist: Nature is brutal by design; Adam could not value the garden, so life shapes us; we believe in God because of evil, not despite it.

outline.heading: Why Allah does not intervene: accountability
outline.gist: He never approves of oppression and never promised to stop each act, but promised a Hereafter with full justice.

outline.heading: Our job to lift oppression and the lens of trial
outline.gist: Removing oppression is our purpose, and everything that happens is a test of gratitude or patience.

outline.heading: Do not ask Allah for motives
outline.gist: Asking why projects human motives onto Allah; the pattern will be clear on the Day of Judgment, so focus on your own role.

outline.heading: Outro

themes.label: Atheism, doubt and responding to disbelief
themes.note: Answers common scientific and philosophical attacks on Islam by exposing the fallacies behind them.

themes.label: Methodology: how to read texts
themes.note: Religion explains the why, not the how; figurative readings of the rib, haste and the sun's prostration; reading verses by Arabic usage.

themes.label: Relationship with the Quran
themes.note: Scientific and numerical miracle claims misuse the Quran, which is a book of sociology, psychology and law.

themes.label: Eman: faith, certainty, doubt
themes.note: Faith must rest on the uniform evidence of the universe, life, history and experience, not fragile claims.

themes.label: Truthfulness and honesty
themes.note: A lie never serves the truth, however well intended.

themes.label: Hadith authority and how to weigh narrations
themes.note: Classes of evidence, isnad and matn, suspending judgment, and a human margin of error in ahad narrations.

themes.label: Trials, hardship and resilience
themes.note: The problem of evil: suffering is part of the design, valued against its opposite, answered by accountability and our duty to lift oppression.

themes.label: Justice and refusing oppression
themes.note: Allah never approves of oppression; full justice comes later and lifting oppression is our job.

quran.point: The sun runs to its appointed resting place; not a claim that it orbits the earth.
Creation in six days means six long periods.
Earth swallowing its water and the sky withholding: the flood was on Nuh's people only.
Man created of haste, a metaphor for impatience.
The Hour draws near and the moon is split, read as a sign before the Hour.
Best stature means fitness for purpose, not physical perfection.
The ant's warning, misused for a glass claim.
A mosquito or what is smaller than it, not something on its head.
Signs on the horizons and in ourselves will appear as knowledge grows.
Three quru' as an example of authentic text with more than one meaning.
Allah destroyed the army of the elephant with birds; do not question what He does or does not do.

hadith.gist: The sun goes after setting and prostrates beneath the Throne, then is permitted to rise again.
Woman was created from a rib.
The splitting of the moon in the Prophet's time, narrated by Ibn Mas'ud.
The blessing in Jabir's small meal that fed everyone, narrated by many companions.
Lying is allowed only in narrow cases such as between spouses and in war.

maxims: Religion explains the why, not the how
Uniformity of evidence
You don't have to defend every single hadith
We believe in God because of evil, not despite it
Everything that happens is a trial

stories.point: A real public miracle was narrated by many companions, unlike the moon splitting.
One who never had a faculty does not feel its loss; we value things only against their opposite.

stories.who: A lion taking over a pride
stories.point: Nature is brutal by design.
Given everything, he could not value it; life's hardship teaches appreciation.

contemporary: Claim that NASA found a split in the moon
Toyota's error-rate benchmark as a model for human error
Surveys on why Muslims leave Islam, with a Yaqeen Institute representative present
The Arab Spring and regime violence driving loss of faith
A recent earthquake killing many thousands
J. L. Mackie's logical problem of evil
takeaways: Do not build iman on claimed scientific or numerical miracles; build it on the universe, life, history and experience.
Read verses by their Arabic meaning and purpose, and recognize figures of speech.
Defend the Quran fully, but treat difficult ahad hadith with a margin of error and suspend judgment rather than lose faith.
See everything that happens as a test of gratitude or patience.
Take up the work of lifting oppression instead of asking why Allah allows it.

_RHIo1KQlOY.speaker: adnan
_RHIo1KQlOY.speaker_note: leads the masjid's Ramadan nights, refers to the cluster summaries he gave in earlier years and to London, Ontario
_RHIo1KQlOY.title: Ramadan 2023, Night 26: Quranic Reflections
_RHIo1KQlOY.one_line: Reflections from Al-Qamar to Al-Hashr: Nuh's hand-built ship against passive waiting, ihsan, the oral Quran, reviving dead hearts, and speaking up against injustice.
_RHIo1KQlOY.summary: He recaps the Al-Qamar to Al-Hadid cluster on gratitude and the balance of spirituality and worldly engagement, and introduces the Madinan cluster from Al-Mujadilah on community relationships. From the description of Nuh's ark as planks and nails he argues that salvation involves human work: a badly built ship sinks whoever is aboard, as Uhud showed, and the ummah's belief that things will 'eventually' work out is a cancer that lets people pray instead of plan. The masjid exists to build the grit for that work. The Quran is made easy for reflection, not just memorization, and becomes a curse if ignored. In Ar-Rahman's question about the reward of excellence he hears Allah saying 'give me your best and I'll give you mine'. The oath by the stars in Al-Waqi'ah leads to the Quran as an oral tradition that book burnings cannot touch, reachable only by a purified heart. Al-Hadid 57:17 is to him the most hopeful verse: Allah revives dead earth and can revive a dead heart, if people put in more than a few nights. The woman who argued with the Prophet shows that speaking up against injustice is welcome.

outline.heading: Opening
The last cluster on gratitude: thank Allah or lose the blessing
outline.gist: Each surah of the cluster ending with Al-Hadid sets up a comparison: be grateful or the blessing harms you on the Day of Judgment, be grateful or it is taken away.

outline.heading: Three endings, and Al-Hadid's balance of spirit and world
outline.gist: Two of the three endings are good if you do what is asked; Al-Hadid seems to offer a choice between spirituality and the material world but teaches a balance, since Muslims cannot leave the world to be run by others.

outline.heading: The Madinan cluster from Al-Mujadilah: relationships in the community
outline.gist: From Al-Mujadilah to At-Tahrim every surah is Madinan and takes an angle on building a Muslim community: dealing with insiders and outsiders, the etiquette of speech and secret conversations, and non-Muslims.

outline.heading: Planks and nails: the ark took years of work
outline.gist: Only here is the ship described by its planks and nails, because it did not simply appear: Nuh spent years building and perfecting it, some narrations say from trees he planted himself.

outline.heading: Waiting for relief is not a Quranic virtue
outline.gist: Rescue is an act of God that involves your contribution. He rejects the circulated narration making waiting for relief the best worship, since a weak report may be repeated only when it adds no new principle, and in the Quran waiting is only for punishment.

outline.heading: A badly built ship sinks: faith gives instructions, not a shield
outline.gist: Mocked for building a ship far from any water, they had to build it well or drown like everyone else; faith explains how to save yourself and is not a protective membrane for those who simply declare they are on Allah's side.

outline.heading: Uhud: being Muslim did not prevent defeat
outline.gist: When the archers ran down the mountain, Hamzah was killed and the Prophet was wounded; having the Muslims on one side was not enough when the job was not done well.

outline.heading: 'Eventually' is a cancer in the ummah
outline.gist: Believing Islam will prevail eventually lets Muslims pray and make dua instead of planning; the only 'eventually' is the day Allah gives no more chances.

outline.heading: The masjid is where we build grit
outline.gist: People lose faith when the miracle does not come; we come to the masjid for the fuel and commitment to see a long job through, as the Prophet planned every detail and tried again after failure.

outline.heading: Made easy for reflection, not only memorization
outline.gist: Dhikr here means contemplation and learning; memorization is how a child reflects. Allah swears He made the Quran easy and asks whether anyone will take it up, then shows the nations who did not.

outline.heading: A blessing that can backfire: answer with your life
outline.gist: The Quran can raise you to the highest rank or be the reason you are punished; its repeated rhetorical question has no written answer because you answer it with how you live.

outline.heading: Which of your Lord's bounties will you deny?
outline.gist: Ar-Rahman counts blessings from start to finish and asks the uncomfortable question again after each one, more than thirty times, never letting you move on.

outline.heading: The reward of excellence: give me your best and I'll give you mine
outline.gist: There is no comparing human best with Allah's best, yet He invites His servant to give his utmost and promises His own in return; it is only a matter of timing.

outline.heading: The frightening reading: I have shown you Mine, where is yours?
outline.gist: Read the other way, Allah has already shown His excellence in every faculty you were given without contributing anything, and asks for yours.

outline.heading: Answering the refrain after every verse
outline.gist: A narration, with some weakness in its chain, gives the reply that none of His blessings do we deny; his teachers paused to say it after every verse, turning a three-minute surah into half an hour.

outline.heading: The oath by the positions of the stars
outline.gist: The Arabs knew and named the night sky better than anyone, yet Allah tells them that if only they knew the enormity of this oath; they had no idea they were looking at stars larger than the whole solar system.

outline.heading: A noble recited Quran: an oral tradition burnings cannot dent
outline.gist: The Quran must be recited aloud; some 35 million huffaz, more than the population of Canada, carry it, passed mouth to mouth from the Prophet for 1400 years, so burning copies changes nothing.

outline.heading: Only the purified touch it
outline.gist: Holding the mushaf with wudu is preferable, but he reads the verse spiritually: only a soul that has worked on its purification connects with the Quran, while a corrupt one misuses it to harm others.

outline.heading: The most hopeful verse in the Quran
outline.gist: Scholars and companions each named the verse that frightened them most and the one that gave them most hope; this is a matter of love for the Quran, not jurisprudence.

outline.heading: Has the time not come for hearts to humble themselves?
outline.gist: Revealed in the first years of Islam, the rebuke sent the companions asking each other what they had done; today hardly anyone is troubled, like the People of the Book whose hearts hardened.

outline.heading: He revives dead earth, and can revive your heart
outline.gist: Placed right after the rebuke, the verse promises that the One who revives dead earth every day will revive a hardened heart; but people must show they want it with more than a few nights a year.

outline.heading: Zihar: a trap that left wives neither married nor free
outline.gist: Declaring a wife 'like my mother' left her neither a wife nor divorced, and objecting made her look as if she belittled his mother; an oppressive practice men devised.

outline.heading: She argued with the Prophet, and Allah heard her
outline.gist: With no ruling yet revealed she kept arguing that this could not be right; the Quran did not rebuke her but said Allah heard her, as in 'Allah hears whoever praises Him', and then forbade the practice. The companions spoke up against injustice whoever they addressed.

outline.heading: If this Quran came down on a mountain
outline.gist: A mountain would crumble in humility and awe, yet the same words wash over a human heart without moving it; something must be missing in that heart.

outline.heading: An ummah that no longer feels revelation
outline.gist: Muslims everywhere have lost the ability to feel and act on what Allah teaches; at a critical point in history they must redefine what it means to be Muslim and how the Quran serves them.

outline.heading: Outro

37:103.en: Then, when they had both surrendered (to Allah), and he had flung him down upon his face

26:62.ar: قَالَ كَلَّآۖ إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهۡدِينِ
26:62.en: He said: Nay, verily! for lo! my Lord is with me. He will guide me

26:63.ar: فَأَوۡحَيۡنَآ إِلَىٰ مُوسَىٰٓ أَنِ ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ ٱلۡبَحۡرَۖ فَٱنفَلَقَ فَكَانَ كُلُّ فِرۡقࣲ كَٱلطَّوۡدِ ٱلۡعَظِيمِ
26:63.en: Then We inspired Moses, saying: Smite the sea with thy staff. And it parted, and each part was as a mountain vast

2:60.ar: ۞وَإِذِ ٱسۡتَسۡقَىٰ مُوسَىٰ لِقَوۡمِهِۦ فَقُلۡنَا ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ ٱلۡحَجَرَۖ فَٱنفَجَرَتۡ مِنۡهُ ٱثۡنَتَا عَشۡرَةَ عَيۡنࣰ اۖ قَدۡ عَلِمَ كُلُّ أُنَاسࣲ مَّشۡرَبَهُمۡۖ كُلُواْ وَٱشۡرَبُواْ مِن رِّزۡقِ ٱللَّهِ وَلَا تَعۡثَوۡاْ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ مُفۡسِدِينَ
2:60.en: And when Moses asked for water for his people, We said: Smite with thy staff the rock. And there gushed out therefrom twelve springs (so that) each tribe knew their drinking-place. Eat and drink of that which Allah hath provided, and do not act corruptly, making mischief in the earth

28:4.ar: إِنَّ فِرۡعَوۡنَ عَلَا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَجَعَلَ أَهۡلَهَا شِيَعࣰ ا يَسۡتَضۡعِفُ طَآئِفَةࣰ مِّنۡهُمۡ يُذَبِّحُ أَبۡنَآءَهُمۡ وَيَسۡتَحۡيِۦ نِسَآءَهُمۡۚ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُفۡسِدِينَ
28:4.en: Lo! Pharaoh exalted himself in the earth and made its people castes. A tribe among them he oppressed, killing their sons and sparing their women. Lo! he was of those who work corruption

28:7.ar: وَأَوۡحَيۡنَآ إِلَىٰٓ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰٓ أَنۡ أَرۡضِعِيهِۖ فَإِذَا خِفۡتِ عَلَيۡهِ فَأَلۡقِيهِ فِي ٱلۡيَمِّ وَلَا تَخَافِي وَلَا تَحۡزَنِيٓۖ إِنَّا رَآدُّوهُ إِلَيۡكِ وَجَاعِلُوهُ مِنَ ٱلۡمُرۡسَلِينَ
28:7.en: And We inspired the mother of Moses, saying: Suckle him and, when thou fearest for him, then cast him into the river and fear not nor grieve. Lo! We shall bring him back unto thee and shall make him (one) of Our messengers

12:21.ar: وَقَالَ ٱلَّذِي ٱشۡتَرَىٰهُ مِن مِّصۡرَ لِٱمۡرَأَتِهِۦٓ أَكۡرِمِي مَثۡوَىٰهُ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَنفَعَنَآ أَوۡ نَتَّخِذَهُۥ وَلَدࣰ اۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ مَكَّنَّا لِيُوسُفَ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَلِنُعَلِّمَهُۥ مِن تَأۡوِيلِ ٱلۡأَحَادِيثِۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَالِبٌ عَلَىٰٓ أَمۡرِهِۦ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
12:21.en: And he of Egypt who purchased him said unto his wife: Receive him honourably. Perchance he may prove useful to us or we may adopt him as a son. Thus we established Joseph in the land that We might teach him the interpretation of events. And Allah was predominant in His career, but most of mankind know not

28:9.ar: وَقَالَتِ ٱمۡرَأَتُ فِرۡعَوۡنَ قُرَّتُ عَيۡنࣲ لِّي وَلَكَۖ لَا تَقۡتُلُوهُ عَسَىٰٓ أَن يَنفَعَنَآ أَوۡ نَتَّخِذَهُۥ وَلَدࣰ ا وَهُمۡ لَا يَشۡعُرُونَ
28:9.en: And the wife of Pharaoh said: (He will be) a consolation for me and for thee. Kill him not. Peradventure he may be of use to us, or we may choose him for a son. And they perceived not

28:10.ar: وَأَصۡبَحَ فُؤَادُ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰ فَٰرِغًاۖ إِن كَادَتۡ لَتُبۡدِي بِهِۦ لَوۡلَآ أَن رَّبَطۡنَا عَلَىٰ قَلۡبِهَا لِتَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ
28:10.en: And the heart of the mother of Moses became void, and she would have betrayed him if We had not fortified her heart, that she might be of the believers

28:11.ar: وَقَالَتۡ لِأُخۡتِهِۦ قُصِّيهِۖ فَبَصُرَتۡ بِهِۦ عَن جُنُبࣲ وَهُمۡ لَا يَشۡعُرُونَ
28:11.en: And she said unto his sister: Trace him. So she observed him from afar, and they perceived not

28:13.ar: فَرَدَدۡنَٰهُ إِلَىٰٓ أُمِّهِۦ كَيۡ تَقَرَّ عَيۡنُهَا وَلَا تَحۡزَنَ وَلِتَعۡلَمَ أَنَّ وَعۡدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقࣱّ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
28:13.en: So We restored him to his mother that she might be comforted and not grieve, and that she might know that the promise of Allah is true. But most of them know not

9:87.ar: رَضُواْ بِأَن يَكُونُواْ مَعَ ٱلۡخَوَالِفِ وَطُبِعَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ فَهُمۡ لَا يَفۡقَهُونَ
9:87.en: They are content that they should be with the useless and their hearts are sealed, so that they apprehend not

9:118.ar: وَعَلَى ٱلثَّلَٰثَةِ ٱلَّذِينَ خُلِّفُواْ حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا ضَاقَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ بِمَا رَحُبَتۡ وَضَاقَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمۡ أَنفُسُهُمۡ وَظَنُّوٓاْ أَن لَّا مَلۡجَأَ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ إِلَّآ إِلَيۡهِ ثُمَّ تَابَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ لِيَتُوبُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
9:118.en: And to the three also (did He turn in mercy) who were left behind, when the earth, vast as it is, was straitened for them, and their own souls were straitened for them till they bethought them that there is no refuge from Allah save toward Him. Then turned He unto them in mercy that they (too) might turn (repentant unto Him). Lo! Allah! He is the Relenting, the Merciful

9:92.ar: وَلَا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا مَآ أَتَوۡكَ لِتَحۡمِلَهُمۡ قُلۡتَ لَآ أَجِدُ مَآ أَحۡمِلُكُمۡ عَلَيۡهِ تَوَلَّواْ وَّأَعۡيُنُهُمۡ تَفِيضُ مِنَ ٱلدَّمۡعِ حَزَنًا أَلَّا يَجِدُواْ مَا يُنفِقُونَ
9:92.en: Nor unto those whom, when they came to thee (asking) that thou shouldst mount them, thou didst tell: I cannot find whereon to mount you. They turned back with eyes flowing with tears, for sorrow that they could not find the means to spend

9:93.ar: ۞إِنَّمَا ٱلسَّبِيلُ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يَسۡتَـٔۡذِنُونَكَ وَهُمۡ أَغۡنِيَآءُۚ رَضُواْ بِأَن يَكُونُواْ مَعَ ٱلۡخَوَالِفِ وَطَبَعَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمۡ فَهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
9:93.en: The road (of blame) is only against those who ask for leave of thee (to stay at home) when they are rich. They are content to be with the useless. Allah hath sealed their hearts so that they know not

OH02LPl_n_4.title: Ramadan 2023 Night 28: Tahajjud
OH02LPl_n_4.one_line: Certainty in Allah shown through Ibrahim, Musa and his mother, then returning to Allah through stories of repentance accepted, ending with the three of Tabuk.
OH02LPl_n_4.summary: Two reminders between rakaat. The first is on yaqin, unshaken certainty and trust in Allah, which he builds from Quranic scenes where every outward means had run out. Ibrahim lays his son down in obedience (37:103). Musa, with the sea ahead and Pharaoh behind, says his Lord is with him and is told to strike the sea, and later the rock (26:62-63, 2:60). Musa's mother, while Pharaoh is killing the sons, is told to put her baby in the river and neither fear nor grieve (28:7); Asiya takes the child in (28:9); and Allah returns him to his mother so she knows His promise is true (28:13). The refrain is that Allah prevails over His affair (12:21). The second reminder is on returning to Allah. He relates Allah's words to Dawud about His longing for those who turned away, and Musa's prayer for rain held back by one man's forty years of sin, a man Allah had concealed and then accepted when he repented. He closes with the three companions who stayed behind from Tabuk, set against the poor believers who wept at being left behind, and whose repentance came after the earth closed in on them (9:118).

outline.heading: Interlude
Yaqin: certainty and trust in Allah
outline.gist: He opens the theme of yaqin and trust (thiqa) in Allah as the core of faith, drawing on Ibn al-Qayyim and Imam al-Haddad.

outline.heading: Ibrahim lays his son down
outline.gist: When both had submitted, Ibrahim laid his son on his forehead (37:103): certainty in Allah's command before any sign of rescue.

outline.heading: Musa at the sea: my Lord is with me
outline.gist: Cornered at the sea, Musa insists his Lord will guide him; he is told to strike the sea and it parts, as later the rock gushes twelve springs (26:62-63, 2:60).

outline.heading: Musa's mother casts him into the river
outline.gist: Under Pharaoh's slaughter of the sons, she is told to place her baby in the river and not fear or grieve (28:4, 28:7); Allah prevails over His affair (12:21).

outline.heading: Asiya takes Musa in
outline.gist: Pharaoh's wife asks that the child be spared as a comfort to them (28:9), while his mother's heart nearly gave way until Allah strengthened it (28:10-11).

outline.heading: Returned to his mother: Allah's promise is true
outline.gist: Allah brings Musa back to his mother so she is comforted and knows His promise is true (28:13), the lesson of yaqin.

outline.heading: Interlude
Allah's longing for those who turned away
outline.gist: Allah tells Dawud that if those who turned from Him knew how He longs for them, they would come back even crawling.

outline.heading: Musa's prayer for rain and the hidden sinner
outline.gist: Rain is withheld because of one man who disobeyed for forty years; Allah, who concealed him all that time, would not expose him on the day he returned, and he repents.

outline.heading: The three who stayed behind from Tabuk
outline.gist: Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayya and their companion stayed behind with those who sit at home (9:87, 9:118), as Bukhari narrates.

outline.heading: Excused by tears, blamed for asking leave
outline.gist: The poor who wept because they had no mount are excused, while blame falls on the wealthy who asked leave to stay (9:92-93).

outline.heading: The earth closed in, then Allah turned to them
outline.gist: When the earth felt narrow and they knew there was no refuge from Allah but Him, He accepted their repentance (9:118), and Ka'b was told of the best day of his life.

outline.heading: Interlude

Doing what Allah asks against every instinct, trusting His promise.

3:31.ar: قُلۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ تُحِبُّونَ ٱللَّهَ فَٱتَّبِعُونِي يُحۡبِبۡكُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَيَغۡفِرۡ لَكُمۡ ذُنُوبَكُمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ غَفُورࣱ رَّحِيمࣱ‏
3:31.en: Say, (O Muhammad, to mankind): If ye love Allah, follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. Allah is Forgiving, Merciful

12:91.ar: قَالُواْ تَٱللَّهِ لَقَدۡ ءَاثَرَكَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡنَا وَإِن كُنَّا لَخَٰطِـِٔينَ
12:91.en: They said: By Allah, verily Allah hath preferred thee above us, and we were indeed sinful

12:92.ar: قَالَ لَا تَثۡرِيبَ عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلۡيَوۡمَۖ يَغۡفِرُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡۖ وَهُوَ أَرۡحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ
12:92.en: He said: Have no fear this day! May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy

MWQrfr2qFvs.speaker: adnan
MWQrfr2qFvs.speaker_note: Ramadan morning series in his usual voice and style, speaking to his own community
MWQrfr2qFvs.title: Attributes of the Prophet: His Forgiveness and Love
MWQrfr2qFvs.one_line: How the Prophet loved openly, above all Khadijah, made every companion feel most beloved, and forgave instantly, even his worst enemies.
MWQrfr2qFvs.summary: In a Ramadan morning talk on the Prophet's character, he takes two traits: love and forgiveness. He argues that modern romance has the concept backwards, ending the story at the wedding, when real love begins only after two people know each other fully and still choose each other. The Prophet's marriage to Khadijah is his proof: twenty-five years through the loss of children and a reversed wealth gap, then fifteen more years of loving her after her death, honouring her friends, reacting to her sister's footsteps, and defending her memory when Aisha belittled her. He separates Muhammad the man, who married one woman for love, from Muhammad the Prophet, whose later marriages united tribes and gave the Mothers of the Believers real autonomy. He then shows how the Prophet made each companion feel uniquely loved, through Amr ibn al-As, Zayd and Usamah, and Muadh, and how he wept openly at his grandson's death, which was unheard of among desert Arabs. On forgiveness, he cites the woman who poisoned him, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, the general pardon at the conquest of Makkah, and Abdullah ibn Ubayy's insult. His point: the Prophet's forgiveness required no persuading; it was always ready. He asks listeners to tell people they love them, stay loyal to spouses, and forgive quickly.

outline.heading: Opening
Following him to be loved by Allah; telling a brother you love him
outline.gist: Love and forgiveness are easy traits to illustrate in his life. Following the Prophet is the path to Allah's love, and he told a man to let his brother know he loved him.

outline.heading: Real love versus romance fiction
outline.gist: School literature and films cut the love story off at marriage, which is exactly where love begins. Loving an image you have built is not love; love is knowing someone fully over years and still loving them.

outline.heading: Twenty-five years with Khadijah
outline.gist: They endured the death of children and an unusual wealth imbalance, and he loved her until his own death, refusing to remarry for years afterwards.

outline.heading: Muhammad the man and Muhammad the Prophet: marriages that united Arabia
outline.gist: The man married Khadijah alone; the Prophet's later marriages joined warring tribes and the house of Abraham, and gave his wives political and religious autonomy, such that Aisha could later lead an army.

outline.heading: Remembering Khadijah: her sister's footsteps and the gifts
outline.gist: He would perk up at her sister's footsteps, and he sent portions of whatever came to his house to Khadijah's friends; Aisha was jealous of no wife but her.

outline.heading: Halting the army for Khadijah's old friends
outline.gist: Near Madinah he stopped the army, spread his cloak for three elderly women and laughed with them, explaining they were friends from Khadijah's days.

outline.heading: Defending Khadijah against Aisha's remark
outline.gist: When Aisha said Allah had given him better, his face changed: she believed him, gave her wealth and bore his children when others did not.

outline.heading: Making every companion feel most beloved: Amr ibn al-As
outline.gist: Every companion felt he was the Prophet's favourite. Amr came home after a successful mission and asked who was most beloved, expecting his own name.

outline.heading: Aisha, then her father: the answer Amr did not expect
outline.gist: The Prophet named a woman, Aisha, which was striking in that culture, then Abu Bakr, and Amr stopped asking.

outline.heading: Zayd and Usamah: the beloved and son of the beloved
outline.gist: The Prophet, anxious at Zayd's late return, rushed to the door without his upper garment. Usamah was so loved that people asked him to intercede.

outline.heading: Telling Muadh 'I love you'
outline.gist: He took Muadh by the hand and told him he loved him before teaching him; how rare it still is for an older man to say this even to his wife and children.

outline.heading: Weeping over Zainab's dying son
outline.gist: He resisted going to the bedside, came at his daughter's insistence, held the dying child and wept, calling it the mercy Allah places in the hearts of His servants.

outline.heading: Why his openness was revolutionary in the desert
outline.gist: Against the hardness of desert Arab culture, a man unashamed to cry or to say he loved people was unheard of, and he opened that door for others.

outline.heading: Forgiving the woman who poisoned him
outline.gist: The poisoned meat at Khaybar affected him for life, yet he forgave her when she admitted it.

outline.heading: Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith and the words of Yusuf's brothers
outline.gist: Ali told the frightened cousin to recite what Yusuf's brothers said; the Prophet answered at once with Yusuf's reply. The Quran's stories are learned so they can be lived when the moment comes.

outline.heading: The conquest of Makkah: 'you are released'
outline.gist: Facing those who expelled him and killed his relatives, he freed them with no strings attached. He taught the dua asking Allah, who loves to pardon, to pardon us.

outline.heading: Abdullah ibn Ubayy and the donkey
outline.gist: He never repaid evil with evil. Riding to visit Ansar families, he was insulted by Ibn Ubayy, whose kingship had been about to be crowned before the Prophet arrived.

outline.heading: Forgiveness that needs no persuading
outline.gist: With him forgiveness was not a process; it was already there the moment the matter was raised.

21:87.ar: وَذَا ٱلنُّونِ إِذ ذَّهَبَ مُغَٰضِبࣰ ا فَظَنَّ أَن لَّن نَّقۡدِرَ عَلَيۡهِ فَنَادَىٰ فِي ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ أَن لَّآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنتَ سُبۡحَٰنَكَ إِنِّي كُنتُ مِنَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
21:87.en: And (mention) Dhu'n-Nun, when he went off in anger and deemed that We had no power over him, but he cried out in the darkness, saying: There is no Allah save Thee. Be Thou Glorified! Lo! I have been a wrong-doer

89:16.ar: وَأَمَّآ إِذَا مَا ٱبۡتَلَىٰهُ فَقَدَرَ عَلَيۡهِ رِزۡقَهُۥ فَيَقُولُ رَبِّيٓ أَهَٰنَنِ
89:16.en: But whenever He trieth him by straitening his means of life, he saith: My Lord despiseth me

21:88.ar: فَٱسۡتَجَبۡنَا لَهُۥ وَنَجَّيۡنَٰهُ مِنَ ٱلۡغَمِّۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نُـۨجِي ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ
21:88.en: Then we heard his prayer and saved him from the anguish. Thus we save believers

21:89.ar: وَزَكَرِيَّآ إِذۡ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُۥ رَبِّ لَا تَذَرۡنِي فَرۡدࣰ ا وَأَنتَ خَيۡرُ ٱلۡوَٰرِثِينَ
21:89.en: And Zachariah, when he cried unto his Lord: My Lord! Leave me not childless, though Thou art the Best of inheritors

21:90.ar: فَٱسۡتَجَبۡنَا لَهُۥ وَوَهَبۡنَا لَهُۥ يَحۡيَىٰ وَأَصۡلَحۡنَا لَهُۥ زَوۡجَهُۥٓۚ إِنَّهُمۡ كَانُواْ يُسَٰرِعُونَ فِي ٱلۡخَيۡرَٰتِ وَيَدۡعُونَنَا رَغَبࣰ ا وَرَهَبࣰ اۖ وَكَانُواْ لَنَا خَٰشِعِينَ
21:90.en: Then We heard his prayer, and bestowed upon him John, and adjusted his wife (to bear a child) for him. Lo! they used to vie one with the other in good deeds, and they cried unto Us in longing and in fear, and were submissive unto Us

21:83.ar: ۞وَأَيُّوبَ إِذۡ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُۥٓ أَنِّي مَسَّنِيَ ٱلضُّرُّ وَأَنتَ أَرۡحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ
21:83.en: And Job, when he cried unto his Lord, (saying): Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy

21:84.ar: فَٱسۡتَجَبۡنَا لَهُۥ فَكَشَفۡنَا مَا بِهِۦ مِن ضُرࣲّۖ وَءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ أَهۡلَهُۥ وَمِثۡلَهُم مَّعَهُمۡ رَحۡمَةࣰ مِّنۡ عِندِنَا وَذِكۡرَىٰ لِلۡعَٰبِدِينَ
21:84.en: Then We heard his prayer and removed that adversity from which he suffered, and We gave him his household (that he had lost) and the like thereof along with them, a mercy from Our store, and a remembrance for the worshippers

2:58.ar: وَإِذۡ قُلۡنَا ٱدۡخُلُواْ هَٰذِهِ ٱلۡقَرۡيَةَ فَكُلُواْ مِنۡهَا حَيۡثُ شِئۡتُمۡ رَغَدࣰ ا وَٱدۡخُلُواْ ٱلۡبَابَ سُجَّدࣰ ا وَقُولُواْ حِطَّةࣱ نَّغۡفِرۡ لَكُمۡ خَطَٰيَٰكُمۡۚ وَسَنَزِيدُ ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ

kLYcDzVUzmM.title: Ramadan 2023 Night 26: Tahajjud
kLYcDzVUzmM.one_line: Reflections on khushu' through the weeping of the Prophet and Abu Bakr, then dua through the door of humility, modelled on the prophets' pleas.
kLYcDzVUzmM.summary: Night 26, with two reminders between rakaat. The first is a set of reflections on khushu' in prayer. He holds up the Prophet, whose chest sounded like a boiling pot from weeping as he prayed, and Abu Bakr, so tender-hearted that he wept whenever he led the prayer. The second is on dua through humility. He opens with a saying he attributes to Imam al-Jilani: every door to Allah was crowded except the door of humble self-abasement, which stood empty, so he entered through it. He then shows the prophets asking in that spirit: the Prophet pleading at Badr until Abu Bakr reassured him that Allah would keep His promise; Yunus calling from the darkness, a dua whose relief is promised to every believer who makes it (21:87-88); Zakariyya asking not to be left alone and being given Yahya (21:89-90); Ayyub appealing to the Most Merciful and being restored with his family (21:83-84). He ends with the Israelites told to enter the gate bowing and ask for their sins to be lifted (2:58).

outline.gist: Ayyub is given back his family and as many again (21:84), and the Israelites are told to enter the gate bowing and ask for their sins to be lifted (2:58).

3:135.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا فَعَلُواْ فَٰحِشَةً أَوۡ ظَلَمُوٓاْ أَنفُسَهُمۡ ذَكَرُواْ ٱللَّهَ فَٱسۡتَغۡفَرُواْ لِذُنُوبِهِمۡ وَمَن يَغۡفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ وَلَمۡ يُصِرُّواْ عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلُواْ وَهُمۡ يَعۡلَمُونَ
3:135.en: And those who, when they do an evil thing or wrong themselves, remember Allah and implore forgiveness for their sins - Who forgiveth sins save Allah only? - and will not knowingly repeat (the wrong) they did

4:15.ar: وَٱلَّٰتِي يَأۡتِينَ ٱلۡفَٰحِشَةَ مِن نِّسَآئِكُمۡ فَٱسۡتَشۡهِدُواْ عَلَيۡهِنَّ أَرۡبَعَةࣰ مِّنكُمۡۖ فَإِن شَهِدُواْ فَأَمۡسِكُوهُنَّ فِي ٱلۡبُيُوتِ حَتَّىٰ يَتَوَفَّىٰهُنَّ ٱلۡمَوۡتُ أَوۡ يَجۡعَلَ ٱللَّهُ لَهُنَّ سَبِيلࣰ ا
4:15.en: As for those of your women who are guilty of lewdness, call to witness four of you against them. And if they testify (to the truth of the allegation) then confine them to the houses until death take them or (until) Allah appoint for them a way (through new legislation)

3:136.ar: أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ جَزَآؤُهُم مَّغۡفِرَةࣱ مِّن رَّبِّهِمۡ وَجَنَّٰتࣱ تَجۡرِي مِن تَحۡتِهَا ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرُ خَٰلِدِينَ فِيهَاۚ وَنِعۡمَ أَجۡرُ ٱلۡعَٰمِلِينَ
3:136.en: The reward of such will be forgiveness from their Lord, and Gardens underneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide for ever - a bountiful reward for workers

3:133.ar: ۞وَسَارِعُوٓاْ إِلَىٰ مَغۡفِرَةࣲ مِّن رَّبِّكُمۡ وَجَنَّةٍ عَرۡضُهَا ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتُ وَٱلۡأَرۡضُ أُعِدَّتۡ لِلۡمُتَّقِينَ
3:133.en: And vie one with another for forgiveness from your Lord, and for a paradise as wide as are the heavens and the earth, prepared for those who ward off (evil)

dIssceS4vJA.title: Ramadan 2023 Night 25: Tahajjud
dIssceS4vJA.one_line: On an odd night of the last ten: the Laylat al-Qadr dua, then Aal Imran 3:135 on turning to Allah right after a sin.
dIssceS4vJA.summary: Night 25, an odd night of the last ten. Before the first rakah he gives a reminder built on Aal Imran 3:135. He begins with the dua the Prophet taught for Laylat al-Qadr, asking Allah, who is Pardoning and loves to pardon, to pardon us, and with the instruction to ask while certain of being answered. Then he works through the verse phrase by phrase: when the people of taqwa commit an indecency or wrong themselves, they remember Allah at once and seek forgiveness for their sins; no one forgives sins except Allah; and they do not knowingly persist in what they did. He explains what the verse means by fahisha, drawing on another verse where the word names a grave sin, and closes with the promised reward of forgiveness from their Lord and gardens (3:136), the same pair the believers are told to race toward (3:133). A later reminder between rakaat returns to Laylat al-Qadr, presenting those who catch it as the true winners.
